topic: How to Forecast Cash Flow for the Next Quarter
objective: Give a practical, simple approach to a 90-day cash flow forecast.

slides.subheadline: Ninety days is enough to see trouble — and act on it.

slides.headline: What does it mean?
slides.body: A quarterly cash flow forecast doesn't need to be complicated. Listing expected income and expenses by month, based on realistic assumptions, is usually enough to spot a coming shortfall with plenty of time to plan around it.

slides.headline: Why it matters
bullet_points: List expected inflows and outflows by month
Use realistic, not optimistic, payment timing
Include known one-off costs like tax or insurance
Update the forecast as the quarter progresses

slides.headline: Key things to know
bullet_points: Compare against last year's same quarter if seasonal
Flag the lowest projected cash point clearly
Decide in advance how you'd respond to a shortfall
A simple spreadsheet is enough to start

caption:
You don't need sophisticated software to forecast the next quarter — a simple month-by-month list of expected income and expenses, built on realistic assumptions, is usually enough to reveal whether a shortfall is coming.

The real value comes from acting on what the forecast shows — deciding ahead of time how you'd respond if the lowest point looks tighter than you'd like.
